gap: No result ChatGPT got (of the three I opened) quotes Apple's own spec lines for the limit that decides this: the M1 MacBook Air drives 'One external display with up to 6K resolution at 60Hz', and the 13-inch M3 Air needs 'Close the MacBook Air lid to use a second external display' — but the cited thedadsneeze.com page already states the same limit in its own words, so the gap is only the primary source and its resolution figures.
standout_why: Compared against thedadsneeze.com (cited), itechguides.com '15 Best' (cited) and wondrik.com (cited); the other results were not opened. thedadsneeze already says M1/M2 Airs support one external display, M3 Airs two only with the lid closed, M4/M5 Airs two with the lid open, and tells readers to check for DisplayPort Alt Mode; it lacks Apple's wording, the 6K/5K 60Hz figures and any link to Apple. itechguides says the port 'must support DisplayPort Alt Mode, Thunderbolt, or USB4 display output' but gives no per-chip display count. wondrik gives one display for base M1/M2 Airs and '5 to 8 watts' for a 1080p panel, but nothing on M3 or M4. None of the three mentions MST. I could not open the Mobile Pixels or FOPO pages or read the Duex Plus DS manual today, so I have no maker-specific mechanism (power draw, USB-A video path, magnet fit) to set against these pages.
decides: It confirms a one-screen extender as the pick for a 13-inch laptop rather than changing it: per Apple, a base M1 or M3 MacBook Air has exactly one external display to give with the lid open, and a single added screen such as the Duex Plus DS uses that one. By inference from Apple's limit (not a FOPO or Mobile Pixels statement I read today), a driver-free two-screen extender such as the FOPO S7 would light only one screen on those Macs with the lid open, while an M4 or M5 Air can run two. This angle does not separate the Duex Plus DS from a freestanding 14-inch monitor such as the ThinkVision M14d; both are one display over one video-capable USB-C port.

findings.label: External displays, MacBook Air (M1, 2020), Apple's spec
findings.value: One external display with up to 6K resolution at 60Hz, alongside the built-in display at full native resolution
findings.source_title: MacBook Air (M1, 2020) - Tech Specs - Apple Support

findings.label: External displays, MacBook Air (13-inch, M3, 2024), Apple's spec
findings.value: One external display with up to 6K resolution at 60Hz with the lid open; 'Close the MacBook Air lid to use a second external display with up to 5K resolution at 60Hz'
findings.source_title: MacBook Air (13-inch, M3, 2024) - Tech Specs - Apple Support
findings.note: Apple's Display Support section. A lid-mounted extender needs the lid open, so the M3 Air has one external display to give in that use; that last step is my reasoning, not Apple's sentence.

findings.label: External displays, MacBook Air with M4 and M5, Apple's support article
findings.value: Up to two external displays simultaneously in addition to the built-in display; 'Closing the lid of your MacBook Air with M4 chip will not increase the number of external displays that can be supported' (same sentence for M5)
findings.source_title: How many displays can be connected to MacBook Air - Apple Support
findings.note: Page is dated March 10, 2026. Apple qualifies the count by the resolution and refresh rate of each display. This page gives no count for M1, M2 or M3.

findings.source_title: Best Laptop Screen Extender (2026): 7 Picks From $90
findings.note: This is why standout is 1: the cited page already carries the limit, without a link to Apple or the resolution figures.
